Issued at 235 PM EDT Thu Jul 30 2026

Pattern / Forecast Synopsis: 

Convoluted weather pattern locally courtesy of a pair of 
disturbances riding a weak point in jet stream flow. Northern wave, 
much more robust with attendant 998mb surface low, will 
continue a south and east progression over Hudson Bay into the 
weekend. Southern wave set to manifest as a convectively charged
wave over South Dakota and Nebraska later today, riding a 
regime of NW flow into Iowa and illinois by the weekend. Cold 
frontal boundary from the northern wave will slowly progress 
south and east Friday into Saturday as the southern wave passes 
to our south and west. Nose of deeper moisture along the front 
will be drawn southward from the frontal boundary into northern 
lower, resulting in budding instability development in an 
environment that will essentially become the neutral point of 
the trough from Friday into Saturday. Weak synoptic flow may 
lead to lake breeze processes becoming the lifting mechanism in 
northeast lower Friday afternoon, with outflow driven convection
spreading westward across the region. Meanwhile, the approach 
of the cold (and soon to be stationary) front will provide 
enough forcing to generate convection across eastern upper. 
Eventually, this front will slowly drift southward into 
Saturday, and should exit by Sunday, with rising (but still low)
500mb heights supporting a period of drier and cooler weather 
into early next week before the next wave passage is progged to 
transpire across the Great Lakes.

Details: 

Today - Tonight: Subtle pre-frontal trough currently analyzed from 
roughly Thunder Bay to Escanaba will provide just enough forcing to 
continue shower and thunder development through the evening across 
those regions, perhaps sending a few showers into NW lower 
overnight, but realistically the better shot of rain by the evening 
into the overnight will first be driven by lake breeze convergence 
processes over eastern upper, and to a lesser extent, northeast 
lower. Surface dewpoints in the low to mid 60s should provide just 
enough to force some diurnal instability. Storm coverage may 
increase in eastern upper later tonight as the stationary front 
increases. 

Friday-Saturday: Influx of deeper moisture (dewpoints anywhere from 
64 to 70) makes its presence known by Friday as the double
barreled systems move closer. Weak westerly flow coupled with 
ample daytime heating should be enough to drum up a Lake Huron 
lake breeze. As instability builds through the day, could see a 
very outflow dominant batch of convection, likely very pulsey in
nature, manifest through late morning into the afternoon. With 
the stationary front drawing closer to eastern upper, greatly 
instability potential supports a better shot at rain up there 
through the day Friday. Resultant stratiform rain with embedded 
downpours to sag southward into northern lower with the advance 
of the front Friday night into Saturday... which may trend a bit
more showery through the day (especially areas south of the 
front, looking at M-55 in particular) before activity wanes into
the overnight hours. Will need to watch how any embedded 
downpours behave over this timeframe. 

Aforementioned deeper moisture plume will balloon PWATS potentially 
as high as 1.75 at the zenith of moisture concentration, which 
suggests very efficient rainfall potential. As such, looking at 
probabilistic guidance, most areas have a 48hr (through 00z 
Sunday) 50th percentile value of 0.40-0.75" of QPF, with the 
highest values favoring aforementioned M-55 corridor, up the 
Lake Huron coast and into eastern upper. 48hr (thru 00z Sunday) 
90th percentile (i.e, only a 10% chance this much rain or more 
falls over that period) tops out at 1 to 2.50" area wide, with 
highest amounts focused on northeast lower and eastern upper, 
which to me, suggests that Friday's convective potential may 
drive robust rainfall in the event the environment supports 
repeated convection. In addition, the lack of forcing conveys 
that not everyone is set to see high rainfall rates. These 
patters are extremely fickle, and area-wide, it would be 
unsurprising to see some areas see less than 0.05" of rain, 
while some localized area sees rainfall in excess of 2.50" over
48 hours. At this juncture, severe potential looks limited to 
storm core collapse processes on Friday when the most robust 
convection is anticipated, and a widespread organized severe 
threat seems unlikely. 

Rest of the period: Cooler Canadian air filters in behind the front 
by Sunday, with cooler and drier weather to kick off next week. 
Seasonable to perhaps above normal temps return Tuesday-Wednesday as 
the next wave approaches, bringing with it, the next rain chances 
after this weekend.
